newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Schroeder angers allies with crime move.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Schroeder angers allies with crime move.

text.p: The leading potential opposition challenger to German Chancellor Helmut Kohl was denounced on Monday as a populist for saying foreigners convicted of crimes were not welcome in Germany.

Gerhard Schroeder's weekend comment appeared to be a bid to boost his Social Democrats' (SPD) reputation on law order -- a traditional strength of Kohl's conservatives -- ahead of a general election next year. But the move alienated many political allies.

The SPD's youth wing said Schroeder, the powerful premier opf Lower Saxony state who regularly beats Kohl in personal popularity polls, was "turning foreigners into scapegoats". It urged the party to disown the comments.

Wolfgang Wieland, leader of the leftist-environmentalist Greens in the capital Berlin, accused Schroeder of cheap pub talk. "Schroeder has changed from being a supporter of civil rights to a supporter of the right-wing," he said.

The debate highlighted a key problem for Schroeder, who has made no secret of his desire to be chancellor and might have a better chance than SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine of ousting Kohl, but is widely mistrusted as an opportunist by many in his own party. A decision on who runs will be made next year.

Schroeder presents himself as a new-style social democrat in the mould of British Prime Minister Tony Blair, and has not been afraid to contradict SPD policy, for instance by saying European monetary union (EMU) should be delayed if candidates flunk the strict economic entry hurdles.

He told Sunday's Bild am Sonntag in an interview that the SPD spent too much time looking at the causes of crime and not enough time fighting it, adding: "Those who violate their rights as guests must leave and without delay."
He also pointed to a wave of organised crime which has come to Germany from eastern Europe since the collapse of communism.
On Monday, the Berlin-based TBB association, representing Germany's two million Turks, and anti-racist groups said Schroeder's comments were irresponsible and could ignite racial hatred.
SPD parliamentary leader Rudolf Scharping defended him in an interview with German Radio, saying he had shown the SPD was taking crime seriously.
But even Kohl's conservatives with their avowed tough line on law and order seemed reluctant to claim Schroeder's comments as an endorsement.

Rupert Scholz, the deputy parliamentary leader of Kohl's Christian Democrats, said Schroeder's move had "revealed him to be an incurable populist...Once more he shows how he changes his political colours to suit himself".
